article.headline: Leaders Clash Over $13.8 Billion Deficit In Only B.C. Provincial Debate
article.summary: BC NDP leader David Eby, BC Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson, and BC Green Party leader Emily Lowan faced off in Wednesday's only scheduled election debate.
article.body:
British Columbia is currently grappling with a record $13.8 billion deficit as party leaders took to the stage to defend their platforms. The debate, moderated by Angus Reid Institute President Shachi Kurl, offered voters their only opportunity to witness the three primary candidates challenge one another directly before the October 24 election.

For voters, the event provided a critical look at how leadership candidates plan to address the province's economic trajectory and the ongoing cost-of-living crisis. With the province facing an existential moment, the rhetoric centered on contrasting visions for economic growth and government priorities, from the management of the provincial budget to the direct financial pressures facing families, such as the rising costs of gas and groceries.

BC NDP leader David Eby defended his record and the timing of the snap election, framing it as a necessary step for British Columbians to move forward. In response, BC Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson pivoted to an critique of Eby’s decade-long record in the legislature, promising to lead his caucus with dignity and unity. BC Green Party leader Emily Lowan utilized her time to distinguish herself as the only candidate who is a current renter and has held a minimum-wage job in the last ten years. She argued that her life experience allows her to better understand the impact of legislative decisions regarding the climate and cost-of-living crises.

As the campaign enters its final stretch, the leaders remain focused on securing support from residents across the province. Voters will head to the polls on October 24 to decide which party will be tasked with navigating the record deficit and the issues raised during the debate.

news.title: Hasan Piker isn't worried about being a political boogeyman this midterms season
news.og_title: Hasan Piker isn't worried about being a political boogeyman this midterms season : NPR's Newsmakers
news.og_desc: President Donald Trump recently called Hasan Piker a “terrible liability” and a “communist.”The California-based streamer — who describes himself as a socialist — has become the GOP’s political bogeyman ahead of the midterm elections. Piker argues those attacks will backfire, but also says he has played a role in being portrayed as a 'figurehead of the insurgent left.'“The way that I'm portrayed in the media is an America-hating communist Islamist fundamentalist who wants to secretly do jihad, and then also, at the same time, very woke and gay, so there's this weird inconsistency in their messaging,” Piker says. “Who I am is very simple. I'm a socialist. I'm an anti-imperialist. I want what's best for Americans, and I want what's best for everyone from all around the world.”In this episode from NPR’s Newsmakers, Piker sits down with host Leila Fadel and argues Republicans are using him to distract from policies that made life less affordable. He also addresses his seven Twitch bans, defends his rhetoric against right-wing reactionaries, and reflects on the crisis of loneliness among young men — and the limits of his influence.“At the end of the day, I'm a Twitch streamer,” Piker says. “I hold no political office. I have no real political power. So getting people to be upset at a Twitch streamer and their affiliation as a, if you want to call it a surrogate, in the primary is going to be very difficult.”Newsmakers is where you'll find NPR's biggest interviews.
